title: The Natural Geometry of Code: Hyperbolic Representation Learning for Program Reasoning
one_liner: Code trees embed more naturally in curved hyperbolic space than flat Euclidean space, because the curved space's exponential growth matches how trees branch.
lead: Code is a tree. When you flatten a tree into a flat sheet (Euclidean space), you stretch and tear it. Hyperbolic space is a curved coordinate system — like the saddle of a horse — where distance works differently and holds trees naturally without distortion. This paper replaces flat embeddings (lists of numbers) with hyperbolic ones and shows programs become easier to compare, complete, and reason about.

paras: Code lives as a tree: each statement branches into smaller pieces, forming a hierarchy. The deeper the tree or the more branches, the more the hierarchy matters. Current models like GraphCodeBERT put these trees into flat space (called Euclidean space — the normal x, y, z coordinates you learn in school). The problem: a flat sheet cannot hold a tree without stretching and tearing.

When you try to cram a branching tree into flatness, related parts get pushed far apart, and distant parts collide. The model loses track of what is important. On deep trees or highly branched code, this distortion is worst. A beginner might try using better coordinates or denser lists of numbers — but no amount of coordinate tweaking fixes the fundamental mismatch, because a tree's branching grows exponentially while flat space's volume grows only by a polynomial, making the gap unbridgeable no matter how you shift the numbers.

callout.html: Flat embeddings distort deep code trees; curved hyperbolic space matches trees naturally.

steps.text: Parse the program into its Abstract Syntax Tree (the AST — a tree diagram of the code's structure).
Place each code piece into a curved space where distances naturally respect the tree's branching depth and width.
Gather signals from neighboring code pieces using paths that respect the curvature, not straight lines.
When deciding which parts matter most, measure closeness along curved paths (geodesics), not flat distance.
Use the embeddings to detect clones, complete code, or predict links — all without distortion.

paras: The paper replaces the embedding space itself. Instead of putting code pieces into flat Euclidean coordinates, HypeCodeNet puts them into hyperbolic space, a coordinate system where the volume grows exponentially as you move outward (like the saddle of a horse).

hidden.h2: The distortion metric: how much the tree gets squeezed
hidden.name: embedding distortion
paras: Embedding distortion measures how far apart two pieces of code stay in the embedding space versus how far apart they should be based on the tree structure. In flat space, deep trees force distortion: close parents and children get spread far apart to make room. Hyperbolic space keeps this distortion low.

The paper estimates distortion implicitly by using the space's native structure: hyperbolic space has a distance formula designed so that exponential branching — the shape of trees — requires minimal distortion to fit.

heat.caption: Darker means more distortion if using flat space. Hyperbolic keeps all levels close.

reads.html: Imagine packing a branching tree into a drawer. Flat drawers force branches to squeeze past each other. A saddle-shaped drawer (hyperbolic) lets branches spread outward naturally without collision.

The paper uses the hyperbolic distance formula's exponential volume growth, which mirrors the exponential size of tree branching patterns, enabling low-distortion embeddings of hierarchical code trees.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: space shape meets code shape
paras: A tree has exponential width: a node with 10 children spawns 10 subtrees, each with 10 more children, yielding 100 descendants at depth 2, 1000 at depth 3, and so on. This exponential growth is the tree's defining shape. Flat Euclidean space has polynomial volume growth: as you go outward, the available room grows like the square of the distance (in 2D) or cube (in 3D). The mismatch is fatal: you cannot cram exponential branching into polynomial space without tearing.

Hyperbolic space solves this by design. In hyperbolic space, the volume available at distance r grows like an exponential of r. This exponential shape matches the tree perfectly. A code piece deep in the tree (far from the root) needs exponentially more room to encode all its descendants. Hyperbolic space provides exactly that room as natural distance, so no tearing occurs. The model then runs standard graph operations — message-passing (sharing information between neighbors) and attention (deciding which parts matter) — but using curved-space distances instead of flat ones. Because the space matches the structure, these operations preserve the code's true relationships.

stages.s: Code Abstract Syntax Tree (hierarchy of statements, expressions)
Convert to hyperbolic embeddings (Lorentz model, numerically stable)
Task solution: clones detected, code completed, links predicted

math.words: The distance between two points in hyperbolic space is defined by the Lorentz model, which uses a special dot product on a curved surface. The distance grows exponentially with the nesting depth, matching tree branching.
math.equation: d_hyperbolic(x, y) = arccosh(-x · y), where x and y are embeddings on the Lorentz manifold
symbols: two code embeddings (points on the hyperbolic surface)
hyperbolic dot product (respects the Lorentz metric)
inverse hyperbolic cosine; outputs the true distance

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Root node and direct child: hyperbolic distance = 1.0 (close, same depth band).
Root node and grandchild: hyperbolic distance = 2.3 (farther, exponential growth kicks in).
Root and deeply nested node: hyperbolic distance = 8.7 (exponential; flat space would need distance ~1000 to separate them).
Same physical distance in flat space squeezes deep descendants together; hyperbolic keeps them spread and distinguished.

math.note: The arccosh function ensures that points at the same tree depth stay close, while exponentially distant depths naturally push apart — exactly matching code structure.

items.html: Flat space handles flat structures fine. Only deeply nested or highly branched code sees the payoff. On simple linear programs, hyperbolic's power is not needed.
Hyperbolic math uses the Lorentz model to stay stable, but care is needed in implementation. Small floating-point errors can push points off the curved surface.

If you build the AST poorly or miss edges, hyperbolic space cannot help, because the whole method relies on the tree structure being correct — wrong edges mean the distance calculations capture the wrong hierarchy, and no coordinate system can recover from that.

items.b: Done right: deeper trees, more gain.
items.html: Test on tasks where structure is deep and branching is real. The payoff grows with hierarchical complexity.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small code dataset with code snippets of varying depth: simple linear code, moderately nested (if-else inside a loop), and deeply nested (triple-nested loops with branches). Embed the code using both a standard flat model and HypeCodeNet. For each snippet, measure the average distance between a root and its descendants as predicted by each embedding space. In flat space, this distance will be compressed for deep nesting. In hyperbolic space, the distance will scale smoothly with actual depth.
demo.metric_eq: depth_fidelity = mean(hyperbolic_distance_to_descendants) / mean(flat_distance_to_descendants); should be >= 1.5 for moderately deep code
demo.closing: The demo should make clear that hyperbolic space naturally handles depth: no squeezing, no collisions, and no information loss.
